BayesTools can generate JAGS [@JAGS] mixed models directly from formulas with random-effect terms.
Its random-coefficient syntax follows the conventions used by lme4 [@lme4], and `prior_random()` allows users to specify the corresponding prior distributions, e.g., random-effect standard deviation priors, correlation priors, variance-allocation priors.

This vignette illustrates how to use the functionality on example datasets distributed with lme4.
The first example uses the `sleepstudy` data and shows random intercepts, correlated and independent random slopes, and Bayes factor tests for the random slope and the correlation, comparing lme4, brms [@brms], and BayesTools.
The second example uses the `cake` data and shows factor random-slope columns.
The third example uses the `sleepstudy` data and shows heterogeneous compound-symmetry, AR(1), heterogeneous AR(1), and continuous-time AR(1) random-effect covariance structures over the study days.
The fourth example uses the `Pastes` data and shows nested random intercepts.
The fifth example uses the `Penicillin` data and shows crossed random effects, compared with rstanarm [@rstanarm].

## Formula Semantics

One major difference from standard R formulas is that BayesTools formulas keeps intercept control and factor contrasts separate.
In a fixed effects formula, BayesTools' `0 + factor` or `factor - 1` fixes the intercept at zero but preserves the factor contrast specified by `prior_factor()`.
For example, an independent factor prior creates one coefficient per factor level, while treatment and mean-difference priors retain their own contrast despite the same no-intercept formula.
(The reason behind this choice is that prior specification, i.e., factor contrast, should not change when other coefficients are modified.)

Random effects specification differs between two types of random structures:

| Structure syntax | Left-side role | Marginal SDs | Correlation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plain bar, `us()` / `un()` | coefficient formula | one per generated coefficient | unrestricted LKJ correlation matrix |
| Double bar, `diag()` | coefficient formula | one per generated coefficient | independent |
| `id()` | coefficient formula | one shared SD | independent |
| `cs()` | one or more discrete indices | one shared SD | one common pairwise correlation |
| `hcs()` | one or more discrete indices | one per index level | one common pairwise correlation |
| `ar1()` / `ar()` | one discrete ordered index | one shared SD | AR(1), `cor^abs(i - j)` |
| `har()` | one discrete ordered index | one per index level | AR(1), `cor^abs(i - j)` |
| `car()` | one numeric-distance coordinate | one shared SD | continuous AR(1), `cor^abs(t_i - t_j)` |

The first three structures operate on coefficient columns.
Their `1`, `0`, and `-1` terms include or remove the random intercept, and their left side can contain continuous slopes, factor slopes, and interactions.
A random factor reuses its already specified fixed effect contrast by default.
Set `random_block(contrasts = c(factor_name = "contrast"))` when the random contrast should be explicit or differ from the fixed contrast.
Therefore `us(0 + group | study)` with an independent block contrast means one correlated random coefficient per `group` level and no random intercept; `0 + group` by itself does not force by-group indicators (as standard R formula does).

The structured CS/HCS and AR1/HAR families operate on discrete index levels instead.
They reject `1`, `0`, `-1`, and block contrast overrides.
They accept factor, character, numeric/integer, or logical columns.
Existing factor level order is retained; otherwise sorted unique values define the levels and AR(1) order.
CS/HCS can combine several indices with `+`; AR1/HAR require exactly one.
CAR requires one finite numeric/integer coordinate, or an ordered factor with numeric labels, and uses actual distances.

### Correlation prior distributions

Correlation priors are completed only after the formula determines the structure and its dimension.
An omitted US/UN correlation prior becomes `LKJ(1)`.
An omitted scalar correlation prior is uniform over the complete admissible raw-correlation interval: `(-1 / (K - 1), 1)` for CS/HCS with K levels, `(-1, 1)` for AR1/HAR, and `(0, 1)` for CAR.
The correlation priors are specified via `random_covariance(cor = ..., cor_scale = ...)`. 
The default `cor_scale = "fisher_z"` places the prior on Fisher's z; `"cor"` places it on the raw correlation and `"logit"` first rescales the correlation from its admissible interval to (0, 1) and then applies the logit transformation.

### Standard deviation prior distributions

Random-effect SD priors have no default and must always be supplied, either once for all blocks in `prior_random(sd = ...)` or per block in `random_block(sd = ...)`.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, results = "hide"}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(BayesTools)
  library(lme4)
  library(rstanarm)
})
```



```{r comparison-helpers, include = FALSE}
compare_sleep_estimates <- function(bayes_model, brms_model = NULL, lme4_model = NULL,
                                    transform_scaled = FALSE) {

  bayes_samples <- JAGS_estimates_table(
    bayes_model, transform_scaled = transform_scaled, random_effects_summary = "standard",
    remove_diagnostics = TRUE, return_samples = TRUE
  )
  bayes_names <- c(
    "intercept"           = "(mu) intercept",
    "Days"                = "(mu) Days",
    "sigma"               = "sigma",
    "sd(intercept)"       = "(mu) sd(intercept)",
    "sd(Days)"            = "(mu) sd(Days)",
    "cor(intercept,Days)" = "(mu) cor(intercept,Days)"
  )
  bayes_names <- bayes_names[bayes_names %in% colnames(bayes_samples)]
  comparison  <- data.frame(parameter = names(bayes_names), row.names = NULL)

  # `||` splits the lme4 random effects into one block per term; only `|` has a correlation.
  if (!is.null(lme4_model)) {
    lme4_vc  <- lme4::VarCorr(lme4_model)
    lme4_cor <- attr(lme4_vc[["Subject"]], "correlation")
    comparison$lme4 <- c(
      lme4::fixef(lme4_model), stats::sigma(lme4_model),
      unlist(lapply(lme4_vc, attr, "stddev")), if (ncol(lme4_cor) == 2) lme4_cor[1, 2]
    )
  }
  if (!is.null(brms_model)) {
    brms_names <- c(
      "intercept"           = "b_Intercept",
      "Days"                = "b_Days_s",
      "sigma"               = "sigma",
      "sd(intercept)"       = "sd_Subject__Intercept",
      "sd(Days)"            = "sd_Subject__Days_s",
      "cor(intercept,Days)" = "cor_Subject__Intercept__Days_s"
    )
    brms_samples <- as.matrix(brms_model, variable = unname(brms_names[names(bayes_names)]))
    comparison$brms <- colMeans(brms_samples)
  }
  comparison$BayesTools <- colMeans(bayes_samples[, bayes_names, drop = FALSE])

  comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 3)
  comparison
}

compare_crossed_estimates <- function(lme4_model, stan_model,
                                      bayes_independent, bayes_allocation) {

  lme4_vc <- lme4::VarCorr(lme4_model)
  lme4_fixed <- lme4::fixef(lme4_model)
  lme4_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"            = lme4_fixed[["(Intercept)"]],
    "sigma"                = stats::sigma(lme4_model),
    "plate: sd(intercept)"  = attr(lme4_vc[["plate"]], "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]],
    "sample: sd(intercept)" = attr(lme4_vc[["sample"]], "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]]
  )

  stan_samples <- as.matrix(stan_model)
  stan_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"            = mean(stan_samples[, "(Intercept)"]),
    "sigma"                = mean(stan_samples[, "sigma"]),
    "plate: sd(intercept)"  = mean(sqrt(stan_samples[, "Sigma[plate:(Intercept),(Intercept)]"])),
    "sample: sd(intercept)" = mean(sqrt(stan_samples[, "Sigma[sample:(Intercept),(Intercept)]"]))
  )

  bayes_estimates <- function(model) {
    samples <- JAGS_estimates_table(
      model, random_effects_summary = "full", remove_diagnostics = TRUE, return_samples = TRUE
    )
    c(
      "intercept"            = mean(samples[, "(mu) intercept"]),
      "sigma"                = mean(samples[, "sigma"]),
      "plate: sd(intercept)"  = mean(samples[, "(mu) plate: sd(intercept)"]),
      "sample: sd(intercept)" = mean(samples[, "(mu) sample: sd(intercept)"])
    )
  }

  comparison <- data.frame(
    parameter = names(lme4_estimates), lme4 = as.numeric(lme4_estimates),
    rstanarm = as.numeric(stan_estimates),
    BayesTools_independent = as.numeric(bayes_estimates(bayes_independent)),
    BayesTools_allocation = as.numeric(bayes_estimates(bayes_allocation))
  )
  comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 3)
  comparison
}

compare_nested_estimates <- function(lme4_model, bayes_model) {

  lme4_vc <- lme4::VarCorr(lme4_model)
  nested_group <- setdiff(names(lme4_vc), "batch")[1]
  lme4_sd_batch <- attr(lme4_vc[["batch"]], "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]]
  lme4_sd_nested <- attr(lme4_vc[[nested_group]], "stddev")[["(Intercept)"]]
  lme4_total_variance <- lme4_sd_batch^2 + lme4_sd_nested^2
  lme4_fixed <- lme4::fixef(lme4_model)
  lme4_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"                  = lme4_fixed[["(Intercept)"]],
    "sigma"                      = stats::sigma(lme4_model),
    "batch: sd(intercept)"        = lme4_sd_batch,
    "cask_batch: sd(intercept)"   = lme4_sd_nested,
    "nested_re: sd_total"         = sqrt(lme4_total_variance),
    "nested_re: var_prop(batch)"  = lme4_sd_batch^2 / lme4_total_variance,
    "nested_re: var_prop(cask)"   = lme4_sd_nested^2 / lme4_total_variance
  )

  bayes_samples <- JAGS_estimates_table(
    bayes_model, random_effects_summary = "full",
    remove_diagnostics = TRUE, return_samples = TRUE
  )
  bayes_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"                  = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) intercept"]),
    "sigma"                      = mean(bayes_samples[, "sigma"]),
    "batch: sd(intercept)" = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) batch: sd(intercept)"]),
    "cask_batch: sd(intercept)" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) cask_batch: sd(intercept)"]
    ),
    "nested_re: sd_total" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) nested_re: sd_total"]
    ),
    "nested_re: var_prop(batch)" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) nested_re: var_prop(batch)"]
    ),
    "nested_re: var_prop(cask)" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) nested_re: var_prop(cask)"]
    )
  )

  comparison <- data.frame(
    parameter = names(lme4_estimates), lme4 = as.numeric(lme4_estimates),
    BayesTools = as.numeric(bayes_estimates)
  )
  comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 3)
  comparison
}

compare_recipe_estimates <- function(lme4_model, bayes_model) {

  lme4_vc <- lme4::VarCorr(lme4_model)
  lme4_sd_for <- function(term) {
    for (group in names(lme4_vc)) {
      group_sd <- attr(lme4_vc[[group]], "stddev")
      if (term %in% names(group_sd)) {
        return(group_sd[[term]])
      }
    }
    NA_real_
  }
  lme4_fixed <- lme4::fixef(lme4_model)
  lme4_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"                  = lme4_fixed[["(Intercept)"]],
    "temp"                       = lme4_fixed[["temp_s"]],
    "recipe[B]"                  = lme4_fixed[["recipeB"]],
    "recipe[C]"                  = lme4_fixed[["recipeC"]],
    "sigma"                      = stats::sigma(lme4_model),
    "recipe_by_replicate: sd(recipe[B])" = lme4_sd_for("recipeB"),
    "recipe_by_replicate: sd(recipe[C])" = lme4_sd_for("recipeC")
  )

  bayes_samples <- JAGS_estimates_table(
    bayes_model, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard",
    remove_diagnostics = TRUE, return_samples = TRUE
  )
  bayes_estimates <- c(
    "intercept"                  = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) intercept"]),
    "temp"                       = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) temp"]),
    "recipe[B]"                  = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) recipe[B]"]),
    "recipe[C]"                  = mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) recipe[C]"]),
    "sigma"                      = mean(bayes_samples[, "sigma"]),
    "recipe_by_replicate: sd(recipe[B])" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) sd(recipe[B])"]
    ),
    "recipe_by_replicate: sd(recipe[C])" = mean(
      bayes_samples[, "(mu) sd(recipe[C])"]
    )
  )

  comparison <- data.frame(
    parameter = names(lme4_estimates), lme4 = as.numeric(lme4_estimates),
    BayesTools = as.numeric(bayes_estimates)
  )
  comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 3)
  comparison
}

compare_structured_estimates <- function(lme4_model, bayes_model) {

  lme4_vc  <- as.matrix(lme4::VarCorr(lme4_model)[["Subject"]])
  lme4_cor <- stats::cov2cor(lme4_vc)
  bayes_samples <- JAGS_estimates_table(
    bayes_model, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard",
    remove_diagnostics = TRUE, return_samples = TRUE
  )

  # AR(1) and CAR estimate one shared SD; HCS and HAR one SD per day.
  if ("(mu) sd" %in% colnames(bayes_samples)) {
    sd_names <- "sd"
    lme4_sd  <- sqrt(lme4_vc[1, 1])
  } else {
    sd_names <- paste0("sd(Days_f[", sub("^Days_f", "", rownames(lme4_vc)), "])")
    lme4_sd  <- sqrt(diag(lme4_vc))
  }
  bayes_sd <- colMeans(bayes_samples[, paste0("(mu) ", sd_names), drop = FALSE])

  lme4_fixed <- lme4::fixef(lme4_model)
  comparison <- data.frame(
    parameter  = c("intercept", "Days", "sigma", sd_names, "cor"),
    lme4       = c(lme4_fixed[["(Intercept)"]], lme4_fixed[["Days_s"]], stats::sigma(lme4_model),
                   lme4_sd, lme4_cor[2, 1]),
    BayesTools = c(mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) intercept"]), mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) Days"]),
                   mean(bayes_samples[, "sigma"]), bayes_sd, mean(bayes_samples[, "(mu) cor"])),
    row.names  = NULL
  )
  comparison[, -1] <- round(comparison[, -1], 3)
  comparison
}
```


## Standard Random Effects Models

The `sleepstudy` data contain reaction times of 18 subjects measured over ten days of sleep deprivation.
We illustrate BayesTools features in a few simple steps: 1) we specify random intercept model, 2) extend the model with random slope, 3) compare the the models using a Bayes factor, 4) specify a model without the random intercept-slope correlation, and 5) test for presence vs. absence of the correlation via a Bayes factor.
For comparison we fit corresponding models with lme4 [@lme4] and brms [@brms].

We standardize the response and the predictor to simplify prior specification for the example.
This allows us to use standard normal priors for the centered intercept and the standardized effect of `Days`, half-normal prior for the residual SD using the scaled outcome, a half-normal prior for random-effect SD, and an LKJ(1) prior for the correlation between the random intercept and slope.
For brms and lme4 we use the explicitly standardized variables defined below, BayesTools allows us to standardize the predictor directly in the model fitting interface.

```{r}
data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
sleepstudy$Subject    <- factor(sleepstudy$Subject)
sleepstudy$Reaction_z <- as.numeric(scale(sleepstudy$Reaction))
sleepstudy$Days_s     <- as.numeric(scale(sleepstudy$Days))
head(sleepstudy)
```

### Random Intercepts

In lme4, a random intercept model is specified using the `(1 | Subject)` syntax in the `lme4::lmer` function.

```{r}
lme4_intercept <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
```
```{r}
lme4_intercept
```

brms uses the same syntax. 
Here we explicitly specify prior distributions for the individual parameters.

```{r}
brms_priors <- c(
  brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept), # intercept
  brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),         # Days_s coefficient
  brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = sigma),     # residual sd
  brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = sd)         # random intercept sd
)
```

brms bounds SDs at zero, so the normal priors on `sigma` and `sd` become half-normal priors.
The model is estimated via `brms::brm` function and `save_pars` allows us to retain all parameters for bridge sampling used later.

```{r fit-brms-intercept, cache_fits = "brms_intercept"}
brms_intercept <- brms::brm(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, prior = brms_priors, save_pars = brms::save_pars(all = TRUE),
  chains = 2, iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, seed = 1, refresh = 0, silent = 2
)
```
```{r}
brms_intercept
```

BayesTools first requires separate specification of the JAGS likelihood and the directly supplied variables (`Reaction_z` and `N`).

```{r}
sleep_likelihood <-
"model{
  for(i in 1:N){
    Reaction_z[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], pow(sigma, -2))
  }
}
"
sleep_data <- list(Reaction_z = sleepstudy$Reaction_z, N = nrow(sleepstudy))
```

The `mu` parameter is specified via a formula that becomes assigned to fitting function's `formula_list` argument later (`sigma` parameter is specified directly in the `prior_list` of the same function).

```{r}
sleep_formula_list <- list(mu = ~ Days + (1 | Subject))
sleep_prior_list   <- list(sigma = unit_sd_prior)
```

The BayesTools formula interface requires specifying prior distributions for the fixed and random effects parameters separately. 
Prior distributions for the fixed effect intercept and predictor enter the fitting function via `formula_prior_list` argument, here specified in the named `sleep_fixed_priors` list.
Prior distributions for the random effects intercept enter the fitting function via `formula_random_prior_list` argument, here specified in the named `sleep_sd_priors` list using the `prior_random` function.
`prior_random()` assigns priors per random-effect block; the block takes its name from the grouping variable, here `Subject`.

```{r}
unit_prior    <- prior(distribution = "normal", parameters = list(mean = 0, sd = 1))
unit_sd_prior <- prior(distribution = "normal", parameters = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), truncation = list(0, Inf))

sleep_fixed_priors <- list(mu = list(intercept = unit_prior, Days = unit_prior))
sleep_sd_priors    <- list(mu = prior_random(Subject = random_block(sd = unit_sd_prior)))
```

The model is estimated via `JAGS_fit` function.

```{r fit-sleep-intercept, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_intercept"}
fit_sleep_intercept <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = sleep_prior_list,
  formula_list = sleep_formula_list, formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = sleep_fixed_priors, formula_random_prior_list = sleep_sd_priors,
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 2000, thin = 5, seed = 1
)
```
```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_intercept)
```

Table below shows close agreement in the parameter estimates from all three packages.

```{r}
compare_sleep_estimates(bayes_model = fit_sleep_intercept, brms_model = brms_intercept, lme4_model = lme4_intercept)
```

### Random Slopes

Adding `Days_s` to the left side of the random-effect term gives each subject its own `Days` effect.
The plain bar `|` also estimates the correlation between the random intercepts and slopes.

```{r}
lme4_slope <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 + Days_s | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
```

brms adds the `class = cor` prior for the correlation; the `class = sd` prior applies to both random-effect SDs.

```{r fit-brms-slope, cache_fits = "brms_slope"}
brms_slope <- brms::brm(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 + Days_s | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, prior = c(brms_priors, brms::prior(lkj(1), class = cor)),
  save_pars = brms::save_pars(all = TRUE),
  chains = 2, iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, seed = 1, refresh = 0, silent = 2
)
```

BayesTools uses the same random-effect term.
`random_block()` adds the correlation prior next to the SD prior; the SD prior again applies to both random-effect SDs.

```{r}
sleep_slope_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(Subject = random_block(sd = unit_sd_prior, cor = prior_lkj(eta = 1)))
)
```

```{r fit-sleep-slope, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_slope"}
fit_sleep_slope <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject)), formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = sleep_slope_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 2000, thin = 5, seed = 1
)
```
```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_slope)
```

```{r}
compare_sleep_estimates(bayes_model = fit_sleep_slope, brms_model = brms_slope, lme4_model = lme4_slope)
```

The estimates above refer to the standardized `Days`.
With `transform_scaled = TRUE`, BayesTools reports them on the original `Days` scale, which we compare with lme4 fitted to the original `Days`.
The intercept, its SD, and the correlation then refer to the first day rather than the mean day.
The random-effect SDs and the correlation differ more: BayesTools reports posterior means and lme4 maximum likelihood estimates, the posteriors are wide and skewed with only 18 subjects, and the priors act on the standardized scale.

```{r}
lme4_slope_days <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
compare_sleep_estimates(bayes_model = fit_sleep_slope, lme4_model = lme4_slope_days, transform_scaled = TRUE)
```

### Testing the Random Slope

Do subjects differ in how their reaction times change over the days?
The Bayes factor comparing the random-slope model with the random-intercept model answers this question.
We compute it in three ways: bridge sampling [@bridgesampling] of the brms models, bridge sampling of the BayesTools models, and a spike-and-slab prior in BayesTools.

brms models are passed directly to `bridge_sampler()`.

```{r bridge-brms, cache_fits = c("marglik_brms_intercept", "marglik_brms_slope")}
marglik_brms_intercept <- brms::bridge_sampler(brms_intercept, silent = TRUE)
marglik_brms_slope     <- brms::bridge_sampler(brms_slope, silent = TRUE)
```

For BayesTools models, `JAGS_bridgesampling()` needs the log-likelihood of the data as a function of the parameters.
BayesTools computes `mu`, including the random effects, and adds the prior densities.

```{r}
log_posterior <- function(parameters, data){
  sum(dnorm(
    x    = data[["Reaction_z"]],
    mean = parameters[["mu"]],
    sd   = parameters[["sigma"]],
    log  = TRUE
  ))
}
```

```{r bridge-sleep, cache_fits = c("marglik_sleep_intercept", "marglik_sleep_slope")}
marglik_sleep_intercept <- JAGS_bridgesampling(
  fit_sleep_intercept, log_posterior = log_posterior, data = sleep_data,
  prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior), seed = 1)
marglik_sleep_slope <- JAGS_bridgesampling(
  fit_sleep_slope, log_posterior = log_posterior, data = sleep_data,
  prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior), seed = 1)
```

A spike-and-slab prior [@kuo1998variable] tests the random slope within a single fit of the random-slope model.
An inclusion indicator switches the `Days` SD between zero (the spike) and the half-normal prior (the slab); with the SD at zero, the model reduces to the random-intercept model.
The `terms` argument assigns the spike-and-slab prior to the `Days` SD only, and `random_monitor(latent = FALSE)` keeps the fit small by not storing the subject-level random effects.

```{r}
sleep_spike_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    Subject = random_block(
      sd    = unit_sd_prior,
      cor   = prior_lkj(eta = 1),
      terms = list(Days = prior_spike_and_slab(
        prior_parameter = unit_sd_prior,
        prior_inclusion = prior(distribution = "spike", parameters = list(location = 0.5))
      )),
      monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE)
    )
  )
)
```

```{r fit-sleep-slope-spike, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_slope_spike"}
fit_sleep_slope_spike <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + (1 + Days | Subject)), formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = sleep_spike_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 5000, seed = 1
)
```
```{r}
JAGS_inference_table(fit_sleep_slope_spike)
```

```{r}
log_BF <- function(marglik_1, marglik_0) bridgesampling::bf(marglik_1, marglik_0, log = TRUE)$bf

data.frame(
  method = c("brms, bridge sampling", "BayesTools, bridge sampling"),
  log_BF = c(log_BF(marglik_brms_slope,  marglik_brms_intercept),
             log_BF(marglik_sleep_slope, marglik_sleep_intercept))
)
```

Both bridge sampling estimates show extreme evidence for the random slope.
All spike-and-slab posterior draws include the random slope, so its inclusion Bayes factor is bounded only by the number of draws.
The spike-and-slab prior agrees with bridge sampling, but it can quantify only Bayes factors that leave some posterior draws in the spike.

### Removing the Correlation

The double bar `||` removes the correlation between the random intercepts and slopes.

```{r}
lme4_independent <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 + Days_s || Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
```

In brms, it also removes the `class = cor` prior.

```{r fit-brms-independent, cache_fits = "brms_independent"}
brms_independent <- brms::brm(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + (1 + Days_s || Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, prior = brms_priors, save_pars = brms::save_pars(all = TRUE),
  chains = 2, iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, seed = 1, refresh = 0, silent = 2
)
```

BayesTools uses the same double bar (or the equivalent `diag()` covariance tag) and the SD prior from the random-intercept model.

```{r fit-sleep-independent, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_independent"}
fit_sleep_independent <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + (1 + Days || Subject)), formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = sleep_sd_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 2000, thin = 5, seed = 1
)
```

```{r}
compare_sleep_estimates(bayes_model = fit_sleep_independent, brms_model = brms_independent, lme4_model = lme4_independent)
```

### Testing the Correlation

The Bayes factor comparing the correlated and the independent random-slope models tests the correlation.
Because `Days` is standardized, the correlation refers to the random intercept at the mean day.
BayesTools does not provide a spike-and-slab prior for LKJ correlations, so we use bridge sampling only.

```{r bridge-correlation, cache_fits = c("marglik_brms_independent", "marglik_sleep_independent")}
marglik_brms_independent  <- brms::bridge_sampler(brms_independent, silent = TRUE)
marglik_sleep_independent <- JAGS_bridgesampling(
  fit_sleep_independent, log_posterior = log_posterior, data = sleep_data,
  prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior), seed = 1)
```

```{r}
data.frame(
  method = c("brms, bridge sampling", "BayesTools, bridge sampling"),
  log_BF = c(log_BF(marglik_brms_slope,  marglik_brms_independent),
             log_BF(marglik_sleep_slope, marglik_sleep_independent))
)
```

Both estimates show strong evidence for the correlation.


## Factor Random-Slope Columns

The `cake` data contain cake break angles measured at ordered baking temperatures for three recipes.

```{r}
data("cake", package = "lme4")
cake$angle_z <- as.numeric(scale(cake$angle))
cake$temp_s  <- as.numeric(scale(cake$temp))
head(cake)
```

BayesTools uses a normal observation model for the standardized angle, and the fixed temperature effect is specified on the standardized scale through `formula_scale_list`.

```{r}
cake_likelihood <-
"model{
  for(i in 1:N){
    angle_z[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], pow(sigma, -2))
  }
}
"

cake_data <- list(angle_z = cake$angle_z, N = nrow(cake))
```

Factor random slopes use BayesTools contrast metadata, but the fixed and random blocks may own different concrete bases.
lme4's `0 + recipe` shorthand expands to one column per factor level; BayesTools instead preserves its resolved treatment basis after `0 +`.
The lme4 comparison therefore defines the treatment-coded `recipeB` and `recipeC` columns explicitly.
Here the random block reuses the treatment contrast established by the fixed `recipe` prior and uses `diag()` so those generated recipe columns have independent random-effect SDs.
In a more complex model, `random_block(contrasts = c(recipe = "..."))` would make a different random basis explicit.

```{r}
cake$recipeB <- as.numeric(cake$recipe == "B")
cake$recipeC <- as.numeric(cake$recipe == "C")

lme4_recipe <- suppressMessages(lme4::lmer(
  angle_z ~ temp_s + recipe + (0 + recipeB + recipeC || replicate),
  data = cake, REML = FALSE,
  control = lme4::lmerControl(check.conv.singular = "ignore")
))
lme4::VarCorr(lme4_recipe)
```

```{r}
recipe_formula <- ~ temp + recipe + diag(0 + recipe | replicate, name = "recipe_by_replicate")

recipe_fixed_priors <- list(
  intercept = unit_prior,
  temp = unit_prior,
  recipe = prior_factor("normal", list(mean = 0, sd = 1), contrast = "treatment")
)

recipe_random_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    recipe_by_replicate = random_block(
      sd = unit_sd_prior,
      monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE, coefficients = FALSE, correlation = FALSE)))
)

recipe_design <- JAGS_formula(
  formula = recipe_formula,
  parameter = "mu",
  data = cake,
  prior_list = recipe_fixed_priors,
  formula_scale = list(temp = TRUE),
  prior_random = recipe_random_priors$mu
)

recipe_design$formula_design$random_effects[[1]]$column_names
names(recipe_design$prior_list)
```

```{r fit-cake-recipe, cache_fits = "fit_cake_recipe"}
fit_cake_recipe <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = cake_likelihood, data = cake_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = recipe_formula),
  formula_data_list = list(mu = cake),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = recipe_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(temp = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = recipe_random_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 4000, seed = 34
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_cake_recipe, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

The outcome comparison uses the same treatment-coded recipe contrasts in lme4 and BayesTools.

```{r}
compare_recipe_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_recipe, bayes_model = fit_cake_recipe)
```

## Structured Random-Effect Correlations

The structured covariances use the levels of a discrete index instead of coefficient columns.
We return to `sleepstudy` and use the day of measurement as the index: in addition to the fixed `Days` slope, each subject receives one random effect per day, and the covariance structure determines how these day-specific effects are correlated.

```{r}
sleepstudy$Days_f <- factor(sleepstudy$Days)

cor_prior <- prior(distribution = "normal", parameters = list(mean = 0, sd = 0.5))
day_random_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    Subject = random_block(
      sd = unit_sd_prior, cor = cor_prior,
      monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE, coefficients = FALSE, correlation = TRUE))
  )
)
```

lme4 2.0-1 and later fits the same structures with `cs()` and `ar1()`.
Note that lme4's `cs()` estimates a separate SD for each column by default and therefore corresponds to BayesTools' `hcs()`, while lme4's `ar1()` and `ar1(hom = FALSE)` correspond to BayesTools' `ar1()` and `har()`.
lme4 uses the `0 + Days_f` model-matrix notation to obtain one column per day.

```{r}
lme4_hcs <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + cs(0 + Days_f | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
lme4_ar1 <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + ar1(0 + Days_f | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
lme4_har <- lme4::lmer(
  Reaction_z ~ Days_s + ar1(0 + Days_f | Subject, hom = FALSE),
  data = sleepstudy, REML = FALSE
)
```

### Heterogeneous Compound Symmetry

The HCS structure estimates a separate random-effect SD for each day and one common correlation across all pairs of days.
For structured factor effects, BayesTools expands the factor into one column per level, so the formula does not use the `0 +` model-matrix notation.
For CS/HCS blocks, multiple index variables such as `a + b` are combined as `interaction(a, b, drop = TRUE)`.

```{r fit-sleep-hcs, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_hcs"}
fit_sleep_hcs <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + hcs(Days_f | Subject, name = "Subject")),
  formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = day_random_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 2000, sample = 5000, thin = 20, seed = 31
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_hcs, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

The table compares the estimates with the lme4 `cs()` fit.

```{r}
compare_structured_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_hcs, bayes_model = fit_sleep_hcs)
```

### Autoregressive Correlation

The AR(1) structure estimates one shared random-effect SD and one adjacent-day correlation; correlations at longer lags are powers of this correlation.

```{r fit-sleep-ar1, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_ar1"}
fit_sleep_ar1 <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + ar1(Days_f | Subject, name = "Subject")),
  formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = day_random_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 2000, sample = 5000, thin = 20, seed = 32
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_ar1, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

The table compares the estimates with the lme4 `ar1()` fit.

```{r}
compare_structured_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_ar1, bayes_model = fit_sleep_ar1)
```

### Heterogeneous Autoregressive Correlation

The `har()` structure combines the previous two ideas: it estimates a separate SD for each day and one AR(1) adjacent-day correlation.

```{r fit-sleep-har, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_har"}
fit_sleep_har <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + har(Days_f | Subject, name = "Subject")),
  formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = day_random_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 2000, sample = 5000, thin = 20, seed = 33
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_har, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

The table compares the estimates with the lme4 `ar1(hom = FALSE)` fit.
The residual SD differs most: with one observation per subject and day, the data barely separate it from the day-specific SDs.

```{r}
compare_structured_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_har, bayes_model = fit_sleep_har)
```

### Continuous-Time Autoregressive Syntax

For irregularly spaced repeated measures, `car()` uses the numeric distances between time values rather than integer lags. The fixed `Days` effect is standardized below, but the CAR time grid remains on the original day scale. Because the `sleepstudy` days are one day apart, the CAR model implies the same covariance as the AR(1) model above, except that the CAR correlation is restricted to positive values; the lme4 `ar1()` fit therefore also serves as its comparison.

```{r}
sleep_car_design <- JAGS_formula(
  formula = ~ Days + car(Days | Subject, name = "subject_days"),
  parameter = "mu",
  data = sleepstudy,
  prior_list = sleep_fixed_priors,
  formula_scale = list(Days = TRUE),
  prior_random = prior_random(
    subject_days = random_block(
      sd = unit_sd_prior, cor = cor_prior,
      monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE, coefficients = FALSE, correlation = TRUE)))
)

sleep_car_design$formula_design$random_effects[[1]]$car$time_values
names(sleep_car_design$prior_list)
```

```{r}
sleep_car_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    subject_days = random_block(
      sd = unit_sd_prior, cor = cor_prior,
      monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE, coefficients = FALSE, correlation = TRUE)))
)
```

```{r fit-sleep-car, cache_fits = "fit_sleep_car"}
fit_sleep_car <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = sleep_likelihood, data = sleep_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = list(mu = ~ Days + car(Days | Subject, name = "subject_days")),
  formula_data_list = list(mu = sleepstudy),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = sleep_fixed_priors),
  formula_scale_list = list(mu = list(Days = TRUE)),
  formula_random_prior_list = sleep_car_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 500, burnin = 500, sample = 1000, seed = 14
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_sleep_car, transform_scaled = FALSE, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

```{r}
compare_structured_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_ar1, bayes_model = fit_sleep_car)
```


## Nested Random Effects

The `Pastes` data contain samples from casks nested within batches. BayesTools supports the lme4 slash notation directly: `(1 | batch/cask)` expands to separate batch and cask-within-batch intercepts. The generated block names are `batch` and `cask_batch`, which can be targeted by a variance-allocation prior.

```{r}
data("Pastes", package = "lme4")
Pastes$strength_z <- as.numeric(scale(Pastes$strength))
head(Pastes)
```

```{r}
lme4_nested <- lme4::lmer(
  strength_z ~ 1 + (1 | batch/cask),
  data = Pastes, REML = FALSE
)
lme4::VarCorr(lme4_nested)
```

```{r}
nested_likelihood <-
"model{
  for(i in 1:N){
    strength_z[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], pow(sigma, -2))
  }
}
"

nested_formula <- list(
  mu = ~ 1 + (1 | batch/cask)
)

nested_data <- list(strength_z = Pastes$strength_z, N = nrow(Pastes))
nested_fixed_priors <- list(intercept = unit_prior)
nested_allocation_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE, coefficients = FALSE, correlation = FALSE),
    allocation = random_variance_allocation(
      name = "nested_re",
      display_name = "nested_re",
      terms = c(batch = "batch", cask = "cask_batch"),
      sd = unit_sd_prior,
      weights = prior("dirichlet", parameters = list(alpha = c(1, 1)))
    )
  )
)
```

```{r fit-nested, cache_fits = "fit_nested"}
fit_nested <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = nested_likelihood, data = nested_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = nested_formula, formula_data_list = list(mu = Pastes),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = nested_fixed_priors),
  formula_random_prior_list = nested_allocation_priors,
  chains = 2, adapt = 1000, burnin = 1000, sample = 2000, seed = 41
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_nested, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

For larger random-effect models, `random_effects_metadata = TRUE` adds the
formula-level random-effect name, grouping label, and random-effect structure. The
same names can be used to restrict the random-effect rows; here we display only
the nested `cask:batch` component. Its SD and variance are reported by
`random_effects_summary = "full"`; the allocation rows (`sd_total` and
`var_prop(...)`) belong to no single block and are therefore not selected.

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(
  fit_nested,
  random_effects_summary = "full",
  random_effects_metadata = TRUE,
  keep_parameters = "random",
  keep_random_effects = "cask:batch",
  remove_diagnostics = TRUE
)
```

The nested lme4 and BayesTools estimates are compared below. The BayesTools allocation rows report `nested_re: sd_total` and the `nested_re: var_prop(...)` values assigned to the batch and cask-within-batch components. Here `name` is the stable allocation identifier and `display_name` is its public semantic owner; set `display_name = ""` when no owner prefix is needed.

```{r}
compare_nested_estimates(lme4_model = lme4_nested, bayes_model = fit_nested)
```


## Crossed Random Effects

The `Penicillin` data set has crossed random intercepts for `plate` and `sample`. We again standardize the response so the same unit-scale priors can be used. This example has no continuous predictor to standardize through the formula interface.

```{r}
data("Penicillin", package = "lme4")
Penicillin$diameter_z <- as.numeric(scale(Penicillin$diameter))
head(Penicillin)
```

The lme4 and rstanarm comparison models are

```{r}
lme4_crossed <- lme4::lmer(
  diameter_z ~ 1 + (1 | plate) + (1 | sample),
  data = Penicillin, REML = FALSE
)
lme4::VarCorr(lme4_crossed)
```

```{r fit-stan-crossed, cache_fits = "stan_crossed"}
stan_crossed <- rstanarm::stan_lmer(
  diameter_z ~ 1 + (1 | plate) + (1 | sample),
  data = Penicillin,
  prior = rstanarm::normal(0, 1, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_intercept = rstanarm::normal(0, 1, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_aux = rstanarm::normal(0, 1, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_covariance = rstanarm::decov(regularization = 1, concentration = 1, shape = 1, scale = 1),
  chains = 2, iter = 1000, warmup = 500, seed = 21, refresh = 0, adapt_delta = 0.95
)
```

The BayesTools formula uses explicit block names because there are two random-effect blocks.

```{r}
crossed_likelihood <-
"model{
  for(i in 1:N){
    diameter_z[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], pow(sigma, -2))
  }
}
"

crossed_formula <- list(
  mu = ~ 1 +
    diag(1 | plate,  name = "plate") +
    diag(1 | sample, name = "sample")
)

crossed_data <- list(diameter_z = Penicillin$diameter_z, N = nrow(Penicillin))
crossed_fixed_priors <- list(intercept = unit_prior)
```

### Independent SD Priors

The most direct specification assigns independent half-normal SD priors to the two crossed random-effect blocks.

```{r}
crossed_independent_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    plate  = random_block(sd = unit_sd_prior, monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE)),
    sample = random_block(sd = unit_sd_prior, monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE))
  )
)
```

```{r fit-crossed-independent, cache_fits = "fit_crossed_independent"}
fit_crossed_independent <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = crossed_likelihood, data = crossed_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = crossed_formula, formula_data_list = list(mu = Penicillin),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = crossed_fixed_priors),
  formula_random_prior_list = crossed_independent_priors,
  chains = 4, adapt = 2000, burnin = 2000, sample = 4000, seed = 2
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_crossed_independent, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

### Variance Allocation Prior

Alternatively, a variance-allocation prior puts one prior on the total random-effect SD and a Dirichlet prior on the fraction of variance assigned to `plate` and `sample`.

```{r}
crossed_allocation_priors <- list(
  mu = prior_random(
    monitor = random_monitor(latent = FALSE),
    allocation = random_variance_allocation(
      name = "total_re", display_name = "total_re",
      terms = c(plate = "plate", sample = "sample"),
      sd = unit_sd_prior, weights = prior("dirichlet", parameters = list(alpha = c(1, 1)))
    )
  )
)
```

```{r fit-crossed-allocation, cache_fits = "fit_crossed_allocation"}
fit_crossed_allocation <- JAGS_fit(
  model_syntax = crossed_likelihood, data = crossed_data, prior_list = list(sigma = unit_sd_prior),
  formula_list = crossed_formula, formula_data_list = list(mu = Penicillin),
  formula_prior_list = list(mu = crossed_fixed_priors),
  formula_random_prior_list = crossed_allocation_priors,
  chains = 4, adapt = 2000, burnin = 2000, sample = 4000, seed = 3
)
```

```{r}
JAGS_estimates_table(fit_crossed_allocation, random_effects_summary = "standard", remove_diagnostics = TRUE)
```

The two crossed-effect fits use the same likelihood and random-effect formula. The difference is only the prior structure: independent SD priors treat the two heterogeneity components separately, while the allocation prior controls the total random-effect scale and estimates how that variance is split. The comparison table mirrors the first example and includes both BayesTools prior specifications.

```{r}
compare_crossed_estimates(
  lme4_model = lme4_crossed, stan_model = stan_crossed,
  bayes_independent = fit_crossed_independent, bayes_allocation = fit_crossed_allocation)
```



### References
